IntroducedBillHeader.Sponsors: House Committee on Criminal Justice & Corrections (originally sponsored by Representatives Kagi and Darneille)

Bill.BriefDescription: Ordering a study of the effect of sentencing structure on prison overcrowding.

BillBody.BillTitle: AN ACT Relating to ensuring that offender populations do not exceedprison capacity; and creating a new section.
BillBody.EnactingClause: BE IT ENACTED BY THE LEGISLATURE OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON:

BillSection.RCWSLText: (1) The Washington institute for publicpolicy, in consultation with the sentencing guidelines commission, thecaseload forecast council, and stakeholders, shall study therelationship between (a) prison overcrowding and (b) the current statecriminal sentencing structure and sentencing ranges. (2) The institute shall determine whether any changes could be madeto the current state sentencing structure and sentencing ranges toreduce prison overcrowding giving great weight to the primary purposesof the criminal justice system. For purposes of this act, the primarypurposes of the criminal justice system are to: (a) Ensure that the punishment for a criminal offense isproportionate to the seriousness of the offense and the offender'scriminal history; (b) Make frugal use of state and local government resources byconcentrating resources on violent offenders and sex offenders who posethe greatest risk to our communities; p. 1 SHB 2105 (c) Promote respect for the law by providing punishment that isjust; (d) Be commensurate with the punishment imposed on otherscommitting similar offenses; (e) Protect the public; (f) Offer offenders an opportunity to improve themselves; and (g) Reduce the risk of reoffending by offenders in the community. (3) The institute shall report its findings to the governor and theappropriate standing committees of the legislature no later thanJanuary 1, 2004. (4) For purposes of this section, stakeholders include, but are notlimited to: (a) The department of corrections; (b) The indeterminate sentence review board; (c) Victims' advocates; (d) Law enforcement; (e) Prosecutors; (f) Defense attorneys; (g) Local governments; (h) Judges; and (i) Groups or organizations interested in sentencing reform inWashington.
